title: Always Put a Baby to Sleep on Their Back
hook: Placing healthy babies on their back for every sleep — naps and night — is the single most effective step to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
key_points: Pediatric guidance: back-sleeping for every sleep, for the whole first year, until the baby can roll both ways on their own.
The 'Back to Sleep' (now 'Safe to Sleep') campaigns coincided with a large drop in SIDS deaths.
Side-sleeping is not a safe alternative — babies can roll to their stomach from their side.
Once a baby can roll both ways reliably, you can let them find their own position, but still start them on their back.
content_html: For newborns and young babies, sleep position is a safety issue, not just a comfort one. Decades of evidence show that placing a baby on their back for every sleep — naps included — substantially lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
extra_html: The public-health "Back to Sleep" campaign (now "Safe to Sleep") of the 1990s coincided with a major decline in SIDS deaths. The AAP advises back-sleeping for the entire first year, started on the back even once a baby can roll. Side-sleeping is not a safe middle ground, because a baby can roll from their side onto their stomach. Once your baby can roll both directions on their own, you don't need to reposition them through the night — but always lay them down on their back. This is general guidance; raise any concerns with your pediatrician.

related.title: A Safe Sleep Space for Baby
related.hook: Pediatric guidance for safer infant sleep is simple: a firm, flat surface with nothing in it — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, or soft toys.

related.title: Crying Is a Newborn's Main Language
related.hook: Crying is how a newborn communicates every need — and a lot of crying in the first months is normal, peaking around six weeks and easing after that.

related.title: Tummy Time: Back to Sleep, Tummy to Play
related.hook: The same babies who must sleep on their backs need time on their tummies while awake — it builds the strength behind rolling and crawling, and helps keep the back of the head from flattening.

flashcards.prompt: In what position do pediatricians recommend putting a healthy baby down for every sleep?
flashcards.explanation_html: Back-sleeping for every sleep is the most effective way to lower SIDS risk. Side-sleeping isn't safe — babies can roll onto their stomach.

flashcards.prompt: When is it okay to let a baby sleep in a position other than the back?
flashcards.back_html: Once the baby can roll both ways reliably on their own. Still place them on their back to start every sleep through the first year.
